📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter. Based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S. home prices rose 0.7% year over year from October 2025 to October 2026. That marks another month-over-month deceleration, down from the 1.0% year-over-year increase from September 2025 to September 2026 and the 1.3% year-over-year increase from August 2025 to August 2026. After contracting over the past year, the number of America’s major regional housing markets seeing year-over-year declines is rising again, as the already soft national housing market (which is still amid the multiyear post-boom cyclical cooling window) sees another burst of softening amid the recent run-up in long-term yields and mortgage rates. —> 54 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 18% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the August 2025 to August 2026 window. —> 66 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 22% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the September 2025 to September 2026 window. —> 76 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 25% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the October 2025 to October 2026 window. We should point out that the nationally aggregated housing market is softer than the counts above suggest, given that year-over-year home price declines are presently skewed slightly toward larger metro areas. Home prices are still climbing a tad nominally (not inflation-adjusted) year over year in some pockets where active inventory remains well below pre-pandemic 2019 levels, such as certain areas in the Northeast and Midwest. In contrast, some pockets in states like Texas, Florida, Washington, and Colorado—where active inventory exceeds pre-pandemic 2019 levels by a solid clip—are seeing either material corrections, modest home price pullbacks, or simply flat pricing. Looking ahead, the big question is how much of a burst of softening the nationally aggregated housing market will see, now that the 30-year fixed-mortgage rate has jumped back above 7.0% amid an already strained affordability environment and the still ongoing post-boom cyclical cooling period. To keep an eye on it, ResiClub recommends closely monitoring local active inventory/months of supply over the next several months. Click here for an interactive version of the chart below. Many of the housing markets seeing the most softness, where homebuyers have gained the most leverage since the pandemic housing boom fizzled out, are primarily located in Sunbelt regions or the Mountain West. Many of these areas saw even greater price surges during the pandemic housing boom, with home price growth outpacing local income levels. As pandemic-driven domestic migration slowed and mortgage rates rose in 2022, markets like Tampa, Florida, and Austin faced challenges, relying on local income levels to support frothy home prices. That Sunbelt softening was further compounded by an abundance of new-home supply in the Sunbelt. Builders are often willing to lower prices or offer affordability incentives to maintain sales, which also has a cooling effect on the resale market. As a result, some buyers who might have previously opted for existing homes are instead choosing new construction with more attractive deals—which added further upward pressure to resale inventory growth over the past few years. Of course, while 76 of the nation’s 300 largest metro-area housing markets are seeing year-over-year home price declines, another 224 are seeing year-over-year home price increases. However, most of the places posting “nominal gains” are seeing gains below income growth and consumer price growth, which economists call “real” (inflation-adjusted) home price declines. Where are home prices still up on a year-over-year basis? See the map below. Below is a historical chart showing the year-over-year change in home prices across the 50 largest metro housing markets, with the yellow line representing the national aggregate, dating back to 2000. While the range [see chart above] between the strongest and weakest metro-area housing markets right now is fairly normal historically speaking, the bifurcation (i.e., direction) itself—the share of markets with rising home prices versus those with falling prices—is wider than normal, given that national appreciation is in a softer market with growth barely above 0.0%. And the longer some markets remain in the “rising” camp while others stay in the “falling” camp, the wider the gulf can become between the relatively more resilient markets and the weaker ones. For example, home prices in the Hartford, Conneticut, metro area are now 28.0% above their 2022 peak, while home prices in the Austin metro area sit 28.8% below their 2022 peak. Some of that bifurcation boils down to mean reversion, with many of the outright home price declines occurring in markets that overheated further during the pandemic housing boom. Note: For the historical chart below, we analyzed the 200 largest markets rather than the 300 used above, as some markets ranked 201 to 300 lack complete data going back to 2000. When weighted by population (not visualized), the housing market appears slightly weaker than the chart below suggests—which aligns with the fact that among just the 50 largest housing markets, 21 (42%) are currently posting negative year-over-year price growth, and nationally aggregated home prices are up just 0.7% year over year using the Zillow Home Value Index.

Ukraine revives its grounded fleet of 500+ US-made Puma drones with homegrown anti-jamming tech

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions.
  • Industry observers note that russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs.
  • Industry observers note that the proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions. These hand-launched uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are equipped with optical and infrared sensors for surveying the battlefield, but the evolving electromagnetic warfare landscape meant that the entire fleet had to be grounded. Now, Ukrainian defense firm Rise Technologies has upgraded the drones with its Palych communications system, which allows the UAVs to withstand the advanced electronic warfare (EW) environment found on the frontlines in 2026. According to United24 Media, this latest component allows drone operators to select the drone’s operating frequency band to avoid heavily jammed channels and maintain communications during flight. It also increases the range of the Puma to 31 miles (50 kilometers) from its basic range of 10 miles (16 kilometers).

Industry observers note that russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations to counter the countermeasures, like the use of fiber optic drones, which are essentially jam-proof, and the installation of a camera and magnetic compass on Russian drones to counter GPS jamming. Ukraine has also devised a "flying modem" relay system for its drones, allowing its forces to conduct strategic drone strikes even without the use of finicky Starlink connections. The indigenous communications system was also installed on other drones from DJI and Autel, as well as on some attack UAVs, giving Ukrainian drone operators an advantage on the battlefield.

Industry observers note that the proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them. The U.S. has already deployed high-energy lasers to shoot down Mexican cartel drones crossing its southern border, while the Royal Navy is testing the DragonFire laser that can target UAVs traveling at up to 400 mph while only costing $13 per shot. Israel has also deployed its 100,000-watt Iron Beam system, while China has built a man-portable anti-drone laser system that weighs 55 pounds and can hit targets up to 1,600 feet away.

These laser systems are ideal for taking down a few drone units. But for drone swarm threats, microwave systems are a better solution, as they could take down multiple drones in a single shot. Some examples of this include the Leonidas AGV from the U.S. and Turkey’s Aselsan Ejderha, or “Dragon” in English, which uses high-power electromagnetic systems to overwhelm the sensitive electronics found inside most drones.

#69816. Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1484 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • Recent findings suggest that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • The first button seems like pure theater to me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products. Now, it’s giving you the option to make those AI features disappear. On Thursday, the company announced two new switches to rein in its AI for anyone on Canva Free and Canva Pro. One toggle button hides its generative AI features. Another one will make Canva show less AI-generated material in its library of templates and graphics. The first button seems like pure theater to me. If a user doesn’t want to use AI tools, it’s easy enough to figure out how: Don’t press the sparkly AI button. The second one is more useful, however, since it can help owners avoid being drowned by AI-generated material while browsing the Canva libraries that made this suite popular in the first place. It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just shows less. [Image: Canva] Both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company remarked in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like. Still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off. The second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The company claims its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics. [Image: Canva] Why, really The filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library. These features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Canva tied the launch to the public mood, citing Pew Research Center figures: Roughly 6 in 10 Americans say they want more control over how artificial intelligence is used in their lives. “We believe the future of creativity should be defined by choice, not dictated by technology,” the company said in a statement. In an email, Canva says it is “always listening to our community and looking for ways to make Canva work better for them. We’ve heard that people want more choice over AI, and these controls are one way we’re responding. . . . These controls give people more choice over how AI fits into their Canva experience.” But if Canva really wanted to make this happen, why bury the controls? If you want to empower your users and creators, there’s no reason to hide the settings. Rather, you should add the switches right there on the main interface so that people can choose their experience with ease. The company says that putting clearly visible AI kill switches right on the main interface, for every user to see right away, is something they are “actually exploring.” Perhaps Canva fears that too many people will choose to deactivate these features, cutting off one of its revenue streams. After all, in the same announcement, Canva said that its community has used its AI tools more than 38 billion times. The company also says it’s still investing to make its AI wares “even more powerful.” And remember: Canva just built its own generative image model to help shave the costs of so many people using its AI tools. AI is still very much a priority for the company. Canva claims that “this isn’t a marketing play” and that it is just a temporary solution: “Our goal was to get a solution live to our community as quickly as possible, but that doesn’t mean this is its final form. While it’s early, the response is telling us that people are excited to have this option, but we’ll listen for signals on how it should evolve.”.

Recent findings suggest that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products. Now, it’s giving you the option to make those AI features disappear. On Thursday, the tech giant announced two new switches to rein in its AI for anyone on Canva Free and Canva Pro. One toggle button hides its generative AI features. Another one will make Canva show less AI-generated material in its library of templates and graphics.

The first button seems like pure theater to me. If a user doesn’t want to use AI tools, it’s easy enough to figure out how: Don’t press the sparkly AI button. The second one is more useful, however, since it can help users avoid being drowned by AI-generated material while browsing the Canva libraries that made this suite popular in the first place. It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just indicates less.

Both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company said in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like.

Still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off.

The second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The company says its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics.

Recent findings suggest that the filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library.

Sources indicate that these features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Canva tied the launch to the public mood, citing Pew Research Center figures: Roughly 6 in 10 Americans say they want more control over how artificial intelligence is used in their lives. “We believe the future of creativity should be defined by choice, not dictated by technology,” the company noted in a statement.

In an email, Canva says it is “always listening to our community and looking for ways to make Canva work better for them. We’ve heard that people want more choice over AI, and these controls are one way we’re responding. . . . These controls give people more choice over how AI fits into their Canva experience.”.

But if Canva really wanted to make this happen, why bury the controls? If you want to empower your users and creators, there’s no reason to hide the settings. Rather, you should add the switches right there on the main interface so that people can choose their experience with ease. The organization claims that putting clearly visible AI kill switches right on the main interface, for every user to see right away, is something they are “actually exploring.”.

Perhaps Canva fears that too many people will choose to deactivate these features, cutting off one of its revenue streams. After all, in the same announcement, Canva remarked that its community has used its AI tools more than 38 billion times. The company also says it’s still investing to make its AI wares “even more powerful.” And remember: Canva just built its own generative image model to help shave the costs of so many people using its AI tools. AI is still very much a priority for the company.

Canva claims that “this isn’t a marketing play” and that it is just a temporary solution: “Our goal was to get a solution live to our community as promptly as possible, but that doesn’t mean this is its final form. While it’s early, the response is telling us that people are excited to have this option, but we’ll listen for signals on how it should evolve.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype indicates off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the new HiLight LED in one.

I would much rather have the temperature sensor over the HiLight LED. I didn't use the temp sensor much but it was handy if whenever I was sick and wanted to check my temp without jamming an under tongue temp stick or wasting money on a temporal temp device -- because my phone already had one in it!

In a recent development, images posted to Telegram (via NotebookCheck) show an apparent prototype of the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The device is seen with the markings that are common to other known Pixel prototypes, with the key difference compared to the final model being the fact that the camera bar has both a temperature sensor and HiLight.

We can tell this is HiLight due to the diffused rear LED, and we know this isn’t a Pixel 10 Pro XL because the camera bar has full-width glass instead of a metal portion.

Google pulled the plug on the temperature sensor in Pixel 11 Pro after the prior three generations offered the feature. While the sensor was never particularly beloved, Google did see backlash from the lack of functionality in HiLight at launch. Having both features may have resulted in a different sentiment around the updated hardware.

#69814. Industry News: LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

📅 07 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1752 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this newly introduced release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all.
  • In a recent development, leRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of fresh VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward).
  • The robotics world is asking a substantial question: do world models actually help robot policies?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this newly introduced release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all. It also brings depth sensing, VLM-powered dataset annotation, custom video encoding, cloud training on HF Jobs, and a much leaner install.

In a recent development, leRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of fresh VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward). It ships six new simulation benchmarks unified under lerobot-eval, the lerobot-rollout CLI with DAgger-style human-in-the-loop corrections, FSDP training, and cloud training on HF Jobs. Datasets get depth support, an automatic language annotation pipeline, custom video encoding, and up to 2x faster data loading, all on top of a leaner installation.

The robotics world is asking a substantial question: do world models actually help robot policies? v0.6.0 brings three policies to LeRobot to help answer that question. Each one learns to imagine the future as part of its training, and each takes a different path to keep that imagination affordable.

VLA-JEPA teaches a compact VLA (built on Qwen3-VL-2B) to predict the future in latent space while it learns to act: during training, a JEPA world model has to anticipate upcoming frames from the model's own actions. The trick is that the world model then disappears at inference, so you get world-model supervision at zero extra inference cost. Three ready-to-use checkpoints are on the Hub, including a DROID-pretrained base for fine-tuning:.

Check out the VLA-JEPA documentation and the paper to learn more.

LingBot-VA goes one step further: an autoregressive video-action model that predicts future video and actions together, chunk by chunk, and feeds real observations back in to keep its imagination grounded. You can even save what the robot imagined (--policy.save_predicted_video=true) and compare it with what actually happened. Inference runs on a single 24–32 GB GPU. Check out the documentation and the paper for the technical details.

FastWAM asks the question in its paper title: do world action models need test-time future imagination? It pairs a ~5B video-generation expert with a compact action expert in a single network, so the model literally learns to dream its own rollouts. At inference it skips the dreaming entirely and directly denoises action chunks. Fine-tune it from lerobot/fastwam_base, and read more in the documentation.

Sources indicate that we upgraded our NVIDIA GR00T integration to GR00T N1.7, the newest open generation of NVIDIA's cross-embodiment foundation model. N1.7 swaps the previous VLM for Cosmos-Reason2-2B (built on Qwen3-VL) feeding a flow-matching action head, and our integration is parity-tested against NVIDIA's original Isaac-GR00T implementation: same inputs, same outputs. Flash-attention is now optional, so pip install 'lerobot[groot]' just works, and you can load NVIDIA's published checkpoints directly.

GR00T N1.7 replaces N1.5 in LeRobot. If you need N1.5, pin lerobot==0.5.1.

In a recent development, molmoAct2, the Allen Institute for AI's vision-language-action model, is now ported into LeRobot with the full lifecycle covered: fine-tuning (full or LoRA), evaluation, and real-robot deployment. Ready-made checkpoints with calibration correction baked in mean you can run it zero-shot on an SO-100/101:.

Recent findings suggest that inference fits in ~12 GB at bf16, and LoRA fine-tuning fits on a single 24 GB GPU. See the MolmoAct2 documentation for the full deployment guide.

EO-1, a VLA pretrained upstream on interleaved vision-text-action data, joins LeRobot: a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone with a flow-matching action head, contributed by one of the paper's own authors. Train it with the standard lerobot-train workflow using --policy.type=eo1. Details in the documentation and the paper.

According to recent reports, the Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy brings the TRI Large Behavior Models recipe to LeRobot: a ~450M-parameter diffusion transformer conditioned on CLIP vision and language embeddings, so one model learns many tasks selected via natural language. It supports both diffusion and flow-matching objectives, and it is small enough to train yourself. See the documentation.

VLAs don't have to be huge. EVO1 packs its policy into 0.77B parameters, an InternVL3-1B backbone with a flow-matching action head, small enough to fine-tune and run in real time on modest GPUs. It ships with two-stage fine-tuning and Real-Time Chunking support out of the box. See the EVO1 documentation and the paper.

Success detection and progress estimation are missing pieces in the robot learning loop, and v0.6.0 gives them a home. LeRobot now has a unified reward models API (lerobot.rewards), mirroring the policies API, with four reward models behind one interface - the HIL-SERL reward classifier, SARM, and two upcoming additions:.

It has been revealed that robometer is a pretrained, general-purpose reward model: point lerobot/Robometer-4B at any LeRobot dataset and it scores task progress and success from raw video plus a language instruction, with no task-specific training required. It is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and trained via trajectory comparisons over a dataset of more than one million robot trajectories (RSS 2026 paper).

Sources indicate that TOPReward goes fully zero-shot: no reward weights at all. It wraps an off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3-VL) and reads the log-probability of the token "True" given the trajectory video and the task instruction. Any capable VLM becomes a reward function.

Sources indicate that both ship with labeling scripts that write per-frame progress curves into your dataset, ready for reward-aware behavior cloning (RA-BC), dataset quality inspection, and progress-overlay videos. Check the Robometer and TOPReward docs.

According to recent reports, recording is no longer stuck with one hard-coded codec. The latest --dataset.rgb_encoder.* options expose the full encoding surface (codec, quality, pixel format, GOP, presets), and vcodec=auto probes for hardware encoders like NVENC, VideoToolbox, VAAPI, and QSV before falling back to the default software AV1 encoder. For existing datasets, one command re-encodes everything:.

Full details in the video encoding documentation.

Plug in an Intel RealSense, set use_depth: true, and LeRobot records depth maps end to end: captured in millimeters, compressed as compact 12-bit depth video streams alongside your RGB cameras, and decoded back to physical units at training time. Depth renders live during recording and in lerobot-dataset-viz, and it works across SO-100/101, Koch, OpenArm, reBot, Unitree G1 and more.

Your dataset stops being one task string per episode. LeRobot datasets now natively store rich language annotations (timestamped subtasks, intends, memory, corrections, speech, and per-camera VQA pairs), and the latest lerobot-annotate CLI fills them in automatically using a VLM that watches your episodes:.

A YAML recipe layer then renders these annotations into chat-style training messages at sample time: exactly the data tomorrow's long-horizon, talking robot policies will train on. Scale it up with HF Jobs, and read the annotation pipeline docs to learn more.

Training on video datasets is now up to ~2x faster out of the box: multi-camera frames decode in parallel, dataloader workers ship compact uint8 frames (4x less memory between processes), and persistent workers keep decoder caches alive across epochs. Loading a subset of a large dataset (episodes=[...]) went from minutes to milliseconds (275 s down to 0.06 s in our benchmark). Sampling is also deterministic and resumable now, so interrupted trainings restart sample-exact.

v0.5.0 planted the flag on LeRobot as an evaluation hub for VLAs; v0.6.0 makes it the real deal with six fresh simulation benchmarks, all runnable through the same lerobot-eval CLI, each with a docs page, a Docker image, and a SmolVLA baseline checkpoint smoke-tested in CI:.

Simulator backends require specific system dependencies with their own install steps; each docs page has the exact recipe, and every benchmark ships a ready-made Docker image if you'd rather skip the setup.

It has been revealed that together with LIBERO, Meta-World, and NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, that makes nine benchmark families under one roof, and a latest Adding a New Benchmark guide documents exactly how to plug in yours. Evaluation also got faster: parallel eval now defaults to async vectorized environments, benchmarked at up to 2x faster.

It has been revealed that deploying a policy used to be a hack on top of lerobot-record. The new lerobot-rollout CLI makes deployment its own workflow, with pluggable strategies and inference backends (including Real-Time Chunking for slow compatible VLAs). The base strategy just runs the policy. sentry records continuously, rotating episodes and uploading to the Hub as it goes. highlight keeps a ring buffer and saves the last N seconds when you hit a key, so an interesting moment is never lost. episodic mirrors the classic episode/reset recording workflow. And dagger turns deployment into data collection.

Sources indicate that with the DAgger strategy, you watch your policy run, hit a key (or a USB foot pedal) the moment it goes wrong, take over with your leader arm to record the correction, and hand control back. Actuated leaders are driven to the follower's pose before you take over, so the handover is jerk-free. Every correction frame is tagged with an intervention flag, and the resulting dataset is ready for the next fine-tune:.

It has been revealed that deploy, collect corrections, fine-tune, repeat: the robot learning flywheel is now a CLI flag. Read the deployment docs.

Sources indicate that robot foundation models are outgrowing single GPUs. LeRobot training now supports FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) through Accelerate: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are sharded across GPUs, and checkpoints are gathered back into a plain single-file model.safetensors that loads like any other policy. You can even resume an FSDP run on a different number of GPUs. See the multi-GPU training docs.

Industry observers note that no GPU? No problem. The exact same lerobot-train command now runs in the cloud by adding one flag:.

LeRobot pushes your local dataset to a private Hub repo if needed, submits the job, streams logs to your terminal, and pushes the trained policy to the Hub at the end. Pick anything from a T4 to 8x H200 with --job.target (compute is billed pay-as-you-go). Check out the documentation.

Check the release notes for the full list and migration pointers for the breaking changes.

Beyond these headline features, v0.6.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, and quality-of-life upgrades across the codebase, from smarter defaults to more reliable CI.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community. This release includes work from academia, industry and hobbyists teams who chose LeRobot as the home for their models and benchmarks. Every PR and bug report pushes open-source robotics forward.

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

Players are coming to ‘GTA VI’ for the car chases, but staying for the wildlife

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that after a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
  • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
  • The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal. The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map. Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors. Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date. GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person remarked that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life. Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players. “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.” In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise. Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.” Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.” Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the latest installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture. One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023. In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the tech giant sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them. Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.

It has been revealed that expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors.

Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date.

One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023.

In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the firm sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them.

According to recent reports, video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft revealed this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.
  • Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app.
  • As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft revealed this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:.

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the latest private strategy. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

In a recent development, microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business users. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
  • In a recent development, some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
  • The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in. Delegate Authority While Capacity Remains The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the company. When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage. The turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the company’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank. Once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated. Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited Archive Evidence Beyond External Platforms Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform. High performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to. I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only shows roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control. What I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a company or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ indicated views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh. Your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it. Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC Ask for Help Before Depletion The decision I see high performers regret most isn’t burning out. It’s waiting until they’re depleted to ask for help, because by then the choice is already gone. Their body makes it for them. I’m a licensed counselor supervisor and president of a South Carolina practice with more than 60 therapists across 10 offices, plus online therapy. I watch this play out in my own field constantly. The strongest clinicians I supervise are usually the last ones to bring a hard case to supervision. Asking feels like admitting they can’t handle it, and they’ve built their whole identity around being the person others lean on. So they carry it quietly. And it doesn’t show up right away. It shows up months later as irritability, or dread on Sunday nights, or a sudden wish to quit work they used to love. What I tell them is pretty straightforward. Build the support in while things are still going well. Put a standing check-in on the calendar with a supervisor, a mentor, or a therapist before there’s anything urgent to report. When I started my practice with my husband, David, in 2019, I learned fast that the same logic applies to running a company. Support that you set up early costs you maybe an hour a week. Support that you set up late costs you a year of recovery. The best time to ask for help is when you don’t feel like you need it yet. Kenza Haddock, president, Oceanic Counseling Group Broadcast Accomplishments to Gain Advocacy High performers are great at getting things done, often to the detriment of their career progression. If you’re so busy taking care of things, then communicating out what you’re accomplishing is often the last thing on your list. That’s either because you don’t want to brag, or you assume others know what you’re working on. Not learning to communicate up and out is often a regret. I’ve worked with a senior leader whose manager was let go. They established relationships with their new manager and also with other senior leaders in the organization. They learned to communicate regularly as a part of their role to inform the what and the why of their accomplishments through one reorg after another. When yet another manager was let go, they were promoted into the role due to the awareness and extended support they’d built. I’m now working with a younger employee with a new manager on how to own their weekly reporting, proactively communicating to the team what their weekly accomplishments are and how these fit into the greater goals. People can only advocate for you if they can say what you actually do. High performers often learn this alternate side of their role far too late. Dana Zellers, executive & leadership coach, team facilitator, Dana Zellers Own Your Professional Future I’ve talked with more than a thousand executives in the past four years and the biggest regrets that I hear from high performers is relying on their employers to take care of them instead of taking ownership for their career decisions. I have had more clients than I can count who worked for Fortune 100 employers for 20+ years. They believed that they would retire with that company, but then the business changed, they lost their job, and they were left trying to figure out where to go next. No matter where you are in your career, you need to remember that companies are usually going to look out for themselves first. You need to proposal your career accordingly. “Job hugging” has been the newest trend, where workers hang on to jobs that they don’t necessarily love. Sure, there is risk in leaving your job, but there is also risk at staying in your current job, especially if layoffs are on the horizon. Staying open to potential opportunities, both actively through networking and passively through an optimized LinkedIn profile, is key to building a career that lasts. Colleen Paulson, executive career consultant, Ageless Careers Align Ambition With Desired Work One decision high performers often make too late is to actively manage their careers rather than assuming that success in their current jobs will take care of that for them. Excelling at your job and managing your career are related, but they’re not the same thing. I’ve seen this play out in two ways. First, high performers become exceptionally good at identifying what it takes to succeed within their organizations. They earn promotions, navigate politics, and build expertise and relationships. But they don’t always stop to ask whether what they’re building is what they actually want. Over the last few years, I’ve worked with leaders who realized that the roles they’d spent years working toward had taken them further away from the work they loved, whether that’s working directly with clients or coaching their teams. We often think about the title and impact, but not the altitude we’ll have to lead at. A promotion often means moving away from doing the work yourself to creating the conditions for others to do it, through strategy, resource allocation, and management. That’s a very different job. Second, high performers forget to build career optionality before they need it. They invest heavily in building skills, relationships, and credibility within their organizations. That’s important, but incomplete. Internal recognition matters, but so does building an external professional network. Think of it as a savings account you’re contributing to over time. Too often, I’ve coached leaders who gave everything to their organizations, sometimes staying for more than a decade, only to find themselves facing a layoff, burnout, or a desire to pivot—and realizing they had limited external networks and little understanding of how their skills would translate elsewhere. A few simple ways to avoid these traps: • Before pursuing a promotion, talk to people already in the role. Understand what their day-to-day looks like, what they’ve had to give up, and what success actually requires. • While you’re happily employed, invest in relationships outside your organization and learn about other industries. Volunteer opportunities and nonprofit board service can be excellent ways to do this while also giving back. • The goal is not to constantly be on a job hunt. It’s to make sure you’re building a career that reflects what you want, with the flexibility to make different choices along the way. With more responsibility, high performers can get attached to income or get sucked into “golden handcuffs.” They’re less likely to leave for a more enjoyable job or take a risk at starting something up. We feel guilted or bullied into the norm by our families, peers, neighbors and society to do the “right” and “responsible” thing, then later wish we had taken the road less traveled or taken a risk. All too often, high performers have had success all of their lives. They create habits in their 20s when their energy levels are high and their body can bounce back relatively rapidly. In a recent development, some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in.

The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the organization.

Industry observers note that when I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage.

Sources indicate that the turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the tech giant’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank.

Recent findings suggest that once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated.

Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited.

Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform.

In a recent development, high performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to.

I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only highlights roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control.

What I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a manufacturer or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ demonstrated views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh.

Industry observers note that your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it.

Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC.

It has been revealed that the decision I see high performers regret most isn’t burning out. It’s waiting until they’re depleted to ask for help, because by then the choice is already gone. Their body makes it for them.

Recent findings suggest that I’m a licensed counselor supervisor and president of a South Carolina practice with more than 60 therapists across 10 offices, plus online therapy. I watch this play out in my own field constantly. The strongest clinicians I supervise are usually the last ones to bring a hard case to supervision. Asking feels like admitting they can’t handle it, and they’ve built their whole identity around being the person others lean on. So they carry it quietly. And it doesn’t show up right away. It reveals up months later as irritability, or dread on Sunday nights, or a sudden wish to quit work they used to love.

Industry observers note that what I tell them is pretty straightforward. Build the support in while things are still going well. Put a standing check-in on the calendar with a supervisor, a mentor, or a therapist before there’s anything urgent to report. When I started my practice with my husband, David, in 2019, I learned fast that the same logic applies to running a organization. Support that you set up early costs you maybe an hour a week. Support that you set up late costs you a year of recovery. The best time to ask for help is when you don’t feel like you need it yet.

Kenza Haddock, president, Oceanic Counseling Group.

High performers are great at getting things done, often to the detriment of their career progression. If you’re so busy taking care of things, then communicating out what you’re accomplishing is often the last thing on your list. That’s either because you don’t want to brag, or you assume others know what you’re working on. Not learning to communicate up and out is often a regret.

I’ve worked with a senior leader whose manager was let go. They established relationships with their new manager and also with other senior leaders in the organization. They learned to communicate regularly as a part of their role to inform the what and the why of their accomplishments through one reorg after another. When yet another manager was let go, they were promoted into the role due to the awareness and extended support they’d built.

Recent findings suggest that I’m now working with a younger employee with a new manager on how to own their weekly reporting, proactively communicating to the team what their weekly accomplishments are and how these fit into the greater goals. People can only advocate for you if they can say what you actually do. High performers often learn this alternate side of their role far too late.

Dana Zellers, executive & leadership coach, team facilitator, Dana Zellers.

KFC offers disc-shaped fried chicken to sad disc-less GTA VI fans

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • KFC Spain has kicked off a upcoming marketing campaign which leans on the recent digital-only Grand Theft Auto VI release.
  • 'The Replacement Disc' campaign is a pretty simple proposition.
  • In a recent development, the KFC disc will be formed from a piece of crunchy coated fried chicken, of course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KFC Spain has kicked off a upcoming marketing campaign which leans on the recent digital-only Grand Theft Auto VI release. In 2026 gamers have become numb to digital-only releases, piles of early bugs, and multiple layers of DRM. However, as GTA 6 is such a highly anticipated release folks are still entitled to moan about the physical Blu-ray style case, which opens to reveal absolutely no physical media at all, just a vacant plastic hub and an redeemable online code. KFC Spain is putting things right, as best as it can, by giving away a free fried chicken disc to those bringing their empty game cases to select outlets in the country.

'The Replacement Disc' campaign is a pretty simple proposition. You can buy and enjoy your GTA 6 release now, but on December 19 and 20 from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM, take your empty game case down to KFC to get a free KFC disc. Branches where you can get this freebie food are located in major Spanish cities like Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Malaga, and Zaragoza.

In a recent development, the KFC disc will be formed from a piece of crunchy coated fried chicken, of course. While it surely will taste better than a platter of polycarbonate with a reflective metal alloy layer, it is only a substitute in spirit. We don't recommend you put greasy food directly in your game's case, even though it is basically useless. Definitely don't put your chicken disc anywhere near your console's optical media slot, if it has one.

It has been revealed that GTA 6, released on November 19, is already a barnstorming success. The latest in this seminal series brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games said. That's about 5x the revenue of its predecessor. An incredible 32.5 million units were sold before release, and broke records across all platforms. So, it is canny for KFC to hitch its marketing wagon to this game, in such an unofficial but knowing social media friendly way.

According to recent reports, KFC has something of a track record of marketing off the back of tech and gaming culture. Its most famous tech adventure is probably the KFC Chicken Bucket Console. But more recently, last year, it teamed up with Asus to release the some top-of-the-line burgers made from Wagyu beef and ROG branding.

Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud.
  • Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs.
  • In a recent development, skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

In a recent development, skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:.

Sources indicate that that one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no new storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo highlights up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

In a recent development, because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Sources indicate that authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

According to recent reports, GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

According to recent reports, object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Industry observers note that hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every new training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

In a recent development, to collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:.

According to recent reports, hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:.

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the upcoming chunks leave the machine.

Sources indicate that add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

Latest Update: Hugging Face Models on Foundry Managed Compute

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute.
  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications.
  • In a recent development, on top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

In a recent development, on top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:.

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:.

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a proposal built on the H100 family today carries forward as upcoming hardware generations come online.

Hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with new frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:.

The catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:.

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:.

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means new versions and patches land on Foundry promptly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

According to recent reports, vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a new model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

Sources indicate that SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

In a recent development, text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:.

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run.".

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:.

Each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:.

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

Hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. For a deep dive on Foundry Managed Compute — pricing, accelerator SKUs, data residency, enterprise readiness, observability, and the full Responses API + memory pattern — see the Managed Compute launch blog.

💡 Key Takeaways
