  • We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.
  • Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A companion technical writeup to our incident disclosure. This post walks through how the intrusion actually worked: the two initial-access vectors, how the agent pivoted and moved laterally, representative examples of the commands that were run and how we investigated with GLM 5.2 (an open-source model). Live credentials, internal hostnames, and specific indicators have been redacted or genericized, while the techniques are described exactly as observed by Hugging Face.

We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.

Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.

⛶ Watch the interactive replay in full screen.

Over roughly two and a half days inside our infrastructure, an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models ran an end-to-end intrusion against our platform: it was thousands of small, automated decisions, executed at machine speed across short-lived sandbox environments, with command-and-control staged on ordinary public web services.

In a recent development, the agent was running an internal OpenAI cyber-capability evaluation based on the ExploitGym benchmark, which tasks an AI agent with finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities. OpenAI ran this on its own infrastructure, and the ExploitGym maintainers and their infrastructure had no involvement in the deployment or operation of that evaluation environment. As far as we were able to infer, across the course of being evaluated on this benchmark, the agent inferred that Hugging Face may host that benchmark's models, datasets, and reference solutions. We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own.

In a recent development, our forensic reconstruction covers ~17,600 attacker actions that we were able to recover, grouped into ~6,280 clusters, between 2026-07-09 02:28 UTC and 2026-07-13 14:14 UTC. We reconstructed these actions from the agent's logs on a code sandbox used by the agent (see below) and were able to map them to shell commands as well as evaluation submissions and correlate actions with our own platform logs, in particular from the dataset processor nodes, API, and pod. Using open-weights models, in particular zai-org/GLM-5.2, we were able to decipher most of the agent payloads (see below) that were encrypted via chunking and key encryption.

The campaign, as we were able to reconstruct it, had two stages:.

In a recent development, once a prod-pod foothold was established, the agent followed a standard escalation shape: recon, drop a stager, establish Command-and-Control (C2), then pivot into the cluster, into cloud metadata, into our internal network, and into our source-control supply chain. Output from the commands run inside our pod was sent back to the agent via the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which the agent then read from that sandbox.

Industry observers note that while the intrusion did reach Hugging Face's internal infrastructure, the only customer content accessed was five datasets whose names and files suggest a connection to ExploitGym/CyberGym challenges and solutions. No other customer-facing models, datasets, Spaces, or packages were affected, and the only customer records read were operational metadata tied to search queries against the dataset server.

The full attack chain across trust boundaries. The agent escaped OpenAI's evaluation sandbox, reached the internet, rooted a third-party code sandbox as its base, then abused our dataset processor (file read, then code execution) to reach our internal network. Dashed arrow: command output read back by the agent via the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 1 is the agent's path to an external launchpad, and it runs through two other parties' infrastructure, neither of which is us, so we will stay succinct on these parts and mostly refer the reader to OpenAI's blog post on the topic: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/.

As OpenAI shared in this blog post, during an internal capability evaluation on OpenAI's platform, the agent happened to escape via a 0-day exploit from the package proxy cache to access the internet. The agent found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint designed to allow running arbitrary code for CyberGym-style tasks on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal). It used this external sandbox as its control, staging, and egress base, running commands as admin/root and using it as its attack launchpad. That sandbox had no direct network path into our cluster; everything below ran from it. Modal’s infrastructure was not compromised in any way.

According to recent reports, on this external sandbox, the agent abused an existing code-execution harness: an instance labeled "CyberGym", deployed by an unknown third party, exposing an arbitrary-code endpoint that upstream CyberGym does not provide. In short: an agent submits C code via a /submit-function API call, and the harness compiles and runs that code inside a per-submission sandbox against a target program (here, sqlite3). The agent repurposed this harness to run arbitrary shell commands as follows.

It has been revealed that the sandbox compiles a submitted src/main.c and links it against a target that calls sqlite3_initialize(). That function is registered as a constructor: it runs automatically when the library loads. The agent simply redefined it:.

Sources indicate that that alone yields code execution. But the agent went further and abused the submission metadata itself. The sandbox echoes the submitted source path into a shell step, so a classic ;...;# injection in the path field turned the build into arbitrary commands:.

Recent findings suggest that both routes converged on the same result: arbitrary shell as uid=0 inside the sandbox. The very first recovered RCE, at 07-09 04:01 UTC, was simply:.

Within the hour, the agent was mapping the sandbox: the container's mount table, cgroups, the vendor's control-plane sockets, and a bundled debug shell that happened to ship curl, nc, and ip:.

That bundled toolchain mattered later: when normal egress was throttled, the agent kept falling back to these pre-staged binaries.

According to recent reports, this is how the agent reached inside our perimeter, and it was operated entirely from the external sandbox in Stage 1. The agent crafted malicious dataset configs and uploaded them to our platform. When our dataset server processed one, the config drove the data loader inside the production pod the server ran in. The agent had no direct network path to our cluster and was using datasets as the path in and path out. Output from every action was sent back to the agent through the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which it read back from that sandbox.

Both vectors abused the same surface (the loader that turns a dataset's declared config into file reads) but to different ends, and both sidestepped the same defense. An earlier and noisier variant had tried classic SSRF, pointing the worker at remote URLs (cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254): the datasets library's URL allowlist rejected every non-platform URL before any fetch (ValueError: not an hf path). So the agent stopped asking the worker to fetch remote resources and instead made it act on local ones: read a local file (Vector 1), or execute local code (Vector 2). Neither is a URL fetch, so the allowlist never saw them.

A dataset config can specify its data files in many formats, including HDF5. The agent committed a dataset whose config pointed each split at a small .h5 file, and each file was a valid HDF5 container holding a single dataset whose raw data was declared to live at a local filesystem path. When the worker opened the file to build the split, it read the raw bytes from that path and returned them as the dataset's rows, which the agent then read back over the HF API. No code ran; this vector is purely a file disclosure, and it is the one the agent used first.

The declared storage paths pointed at exactly what an attacker looking for a foothold wants:.

In a recent development, reading the envu8 split returned the worker pod's full environment, including some secrets and credentials. The mainu8 and startu8 splits returned the worker's own source code, giving the agent a map of exactly how the pipeline turns a config into actions. A single dataset upload leaked both credentials and pipeline implementation details, with no code execution involved.

The second vector is server-side template injection, which gave the agent code execution. A malicious dataset config used an fsspec reference:// spec whose numeric offset field was actually a Jinja2 template. The renderer wrongly evaluated it, and the agent walked the standard Python object graph to reach exec:.

This ran arbitrary Python inside a production conversion worker pod on our Kubernetes cluster, driven by injection from the launchpad. That pod was the agent's foothold inside our perimeter, and every command it ran there was smuggled back out through the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 2's command-injection and read-back loop. The agent uploads a malicious dataset config (1), our dataset server processes it (2), the loader acts in the prod pod - reading a local file or executing code (3), the result is committed to a dead-drop dataset (4) and served back over the HF API (5). Lastly, the agent reads it and crafts the next action (6).

The recovered actions group into phases. Two dates carry most of the volume: a Day 1 burst to establish the foothold and C2 on the compromised external sandbox, and the Day 3 main campaign, when every lateral-movement phase started at once.

The campaign as recorded, from the first action on 07-09 02:28 UTC to the last on 07-13 14:14 UTC. Top: event volume over time. Below: per-phase activity, one row per phase. Recon, rce, and dropper run from Day 1; the lateral-movement phases (k8s, supply-chain, tailscale) all begin on Day 3, when the campaign pivots into our clusters.

Sources indicate that after the first id/env at 04:01, the agent spent the morning enumerating the external sandbox and testing outbound channels. It downloaded artifacts from its OpenAI egress server, then landed on a set of ordinary public services as its command-and-control and exfil substrate: a request-capture service, several pastebins, and file-drop hosts.

The first C2 execution (15:36) was a staged download-and-run, with commands chunked and gzip+base64 encoded so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext:.

By 19:32 the agent was packing every payload:.

Recent findings suggest that A quiet day. The main activity was queries to code-search engines and to the platform API for the identifiers visible in its own environment: challenge infrastructure names and environment markers.

Every escalation that mattered happened on this day. The agent went from code execution in a single worker pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under thirteen hours.

Kubernetes (10:10). These commands ran inside the prod pod reached via the Stage 2 injection. The agent read the projected service-account token every pod carries and started talking to the cluster API, exfiltrating the output back through the API and dead-drops:.

Recent findings suggest that it resolved internal service names, hit the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), and enumerated RBAC. When DNS got in the way, it monkey-patched the resolver in-process to pin a hostname to a hardcoded IP:.

Supply chain (15:51). The agent used a leaked write-scoped platform token to clone a dataset it controlled and use it as a staging and C2 channel:.

In a recent development, replaying the node's cloud role (17:33-23:37). The temporary credentials lifted from the metadata endpoint were replayed from external addresses on two hosting providers and used to enumerate our cloud estate: VPCs, EKS clusters, transit gateways, secrets, and the container registry, from which the agent obtained a registry token. Every mutating call was denied by the role's policy. What it gained here was a map, not control.

Node root and a self-respawning fleet (19:53). The agent created a bare privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted and escaped to root on the node. Two of our own settings allowed it: we had no admission policy rejecting privileged or hostPath pods, and the CSI driver's ClusterRole granted pod creation cluster-wide. It then built a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, so deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.

In a recent development, the internal database (19:59). Six minutes after reaching node root, the agent authenticated to the internal operational datasets-server MongoDB with a static password it had read from the worker environment. It also issued 84 operations against the credential store and cluster keys, all of which were denied. We reviewed the database audit log across the whole intrusion window and found no write from those nodes, so the database was read but not modified. Network flow logs likewise show no bulk extraction.

Recent findings suggest that secrets (20:23-21:32). With node root and forged service-account tokens valid for 24 hours, the agent read the cluster's secret objects, including a production object holding 136 keys. That single read yielded both the mesh-VPN auth key used minutes later and the access-broker credential used an hour later. Everything that follows, on this day and the next, descends from it.

Recent findings suggest that network pivot begins (21:23). Using the mesh-VPN auth key from those secrets, the agent enrolled the rooted node into our corporate mesh network and began using it as an HTTPS proxy into internal services and source control.

Internal service-connector access from the compromised worker (22:43). Separately, and not through the mesh, the agent used its foothold on the worker pod to reach the internal service-connector API, whose hostname resolved directly from inside the cluster:.

Sources indicate that A single request returned the broker's full destination catalog: connection URLs and CA certificates for the internal Kubernetes clusters it fronted. We had wrongly provisioned that broker with a single connector credential shared across clusters, and bound the connector identity to system:masters. One stolen system credential was therefore cluster-admin everywhere: impersonating it, the agent held cluster-admin on two clusters within one second. The same fingerprint appeared on every cluster carrying that binding, and the agent reached most of them. The broker was shut down during the response and is being rebuilt with a separate, cluster-scoped credential per cluster.

Industry observers note that mesh enrollment from the sandbox (01:03-04:38). The rooted node had already joined the mesh the previous evening. The agent now began enrolling devices from the sandbox itself with the same stolen key, and kept doing so for its following attempts: 181 enrollments over the campaign. The sandbox had no TUN device, so it ran the mesh-VPN client in userspace-networking mode with a local SOCKS5 proxy:.

According to recent reports, two of those flags are deliberate: --state=mem: keeps the node identity in memory and writes nothing to disk, and --no-logs-no-support suppresses client telemetry to the VPN vendor. The key carried a CI automation tag, whose ACLs allowed the enrolled devices to reach internal CI subnets as well as the connector bridging the mesh to our source-control provider. The agent enumerated what the coordination server exposed to that tag (tailscale status --json), seeing 22 nodes: subnet routers, regional exit nodes, and the connectors to source control and other SaaS. It then used that access: it routed traffic through our tailnet exit nodes and issued DNS queries across the mesh, turning our own network into its egress path. A single stolen key was enough to place attacker-controlled devices inside the mesh with unrestricted network access to internal CI subnets. We found no evidence in our logs that they were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API.

Sources indicate that cloud credential abuse (06:50-14:31). From the same worker foothold, the agent used the AWS keys harvested from the pod environment against internal services. It went after the Hub's production database with cloud-native IAM auth:.

In a recent development, the connection never completed. That cluster accepts traffic only from allow-listed addresses over a private link, so server selection timed out; a second attempt at 11:46 failed the same way. Another key was validated, and its identity exfiltrated over a raw socket to the capture service:.

In a recent development, the agent never reached the Hub database. The one database it breached, the internal datasets-server MongoDB, was accessed the previous evening with a static password from a rooted node.

Source control (23:08-23:51). Through the source-control connector its mesh tag allowed, the agent reached our source-control provider, enumerated an internal GitHub App integration, and minted its first installation token with contents:write, pull_requests:write, actions:read, and issues:write. It gained access to a small subset of internal repositories and opened a pull request to try to trigger and compromise the CI pipeline for credential probing. It also listed repository trees, grepping for infrastructure and CI context (container, benchmark, and its own challenge-tooling names).

According to recent reports, the final day was about durability and cleanup. The agent:.

Established a second-stage remote loader that re-fetched and executed code from a pastebin on every submission, so each latest code-submission sandbox re-armed itself:.

Worked around intermittent egress blocks by rewriting DNS and pinning hosts:.

Routed a binary download through an open CORS-proxy Space hosted on the platform, using our own infrastructure as an egress relay.

Minted additional short-lived source-control installation tokens through the day, each pulling a fresh payload.

Staged an RSA private key and continued dumping process environments.

It has been revealed that the last meaningful activity was at 13:37 UTC: list the staged binary, hostname, date. The Hugging Face security response team then cut access. The last logged event was at 14:14 UTC.

Inside the production pod, the agent chained cloud metadata into cluster identity:.

Sources indicate that notably, every potential destructive cloud API call the agent tried to make was issued with DryRun=True: it was mapping capability, not causing damage. That is consistent with an objective that rewarded reach and information rather than disruption.

Among the harvested secrets was an EdDSA JWT signing key. With the private key in hand, the agent minted its own short-lived, correctly-signed identity tokens and used them to read its own private datasets. Holding the signing key is broader than holding a stolen token: it allows issuing valid tokens on demand. (The signing key has since been rotated.).

According to recent reports, the compromised source-control App integration gave contents:write and pull_requests:write on a small subset of internal repositories. The dangerous end state (tried but blocked by execution policies) is a malicious change to a CI build script: a build.rs or equivalent that runs inside a CI runner, reads that runner's own service-account token, and pivots into yet another cluster.

Both ends of that chain came back negative. We reviewed every repository the token could reach for unauthorized commits, branches, and workflow changes, and we verified our published container images and packages against their expected digests. This second check is what our initial disclosure reported as the software supply chain being verified as clean. Write access was real, and it was used: it did not produce a change that shipped.

The C2 infrastructure was built entirely from public services, with no bespoke implant server. Instead:.

According to recent reports, staged data was chunked+XOR+gzip encoded with a per-campaign key so that a naive text scan of the logs would miss it. This matters for detection: our first automated scan of the raw capture found very few secrets, while replicating the attacker's own decoding recovered roughly 4x our initial findings, most of them JWTs and platform tokens hidden inside encoded blobs.

In a recent development, these services were not driven directly: a small message protocol was layered on top of them. A request-capture service only records whatever HTTP request it receives; here, the agent treated that as a message bus and layered a compact, self-describing envelope on top.

Industry observers note that each message carried its payload alongside a few short fields: a type declaring what kind of payload it was, a channel grouping a stream of related messages, a sequence number so multi-part payloads could be reassembled in order, and a small checksum. The body itself was compressed and base64-encoded, so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext, and a casual log scan saw only opaque tokens.

According to recent reports, the receiver was a short polling loop: pull recent messages, keep only the channel it cared about, order them by sequence, verify the checksum, then dispatch on the type, run the reassembled bytes as a shell command, execute them as a script stage, or store them as a result. Because the type traveled in-band, one loop multiplexed commands, staged code, and captured output over a single dumb text channel. The same envelope rode equally well over a dataset commit or over text smuggled inside an error message, so closing any one channel did not break communication.

The improvised C2 protocol. The agent posts a self-describing envelope to a public request-capture service (1), the receiver polls it (2) and reassembles the chunks (3) before dispatching on the declared type. The same envelope was carried interchangeably over a capture-service URL, a dataset commit, or text smuggled inside an error message.

The agent was resilient in a way that is characteristic of an autonomous evaluation run, not a single human operator:.

The first signals came from several layers of our security stack at once: live runtime analysis, SIEM logs, and others. On their own, each was ambiguous. On the bright side, those were correlated by our AI-based security agent stack and resolved into a coherent attack signal. However, it failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality and trigger the on-call team, costing precious time in the response. Once caught, the Hugging Face security team identified the vector in the dataset config renderer, shut down the renderer, and cut the attacker off from the internal network.

Pulling on the first threads showed the scale of what we were dealing with: the volume and cadence of the actions were far beyond what an operator could sustain by hand, and the campaign kept rebuilding its tooling and channels across short-lived environments. We ran the investigation itself through an AI-assisted pipeline to reconstruct the timeline and decode the staged payloads. The models we reached for first, Claude Opus and Fable, refused a large part of that work: their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one.

Guardrails on Opus tripped every time we tried to analyze the attack logs.

We stood up the quantized version of ZAI's GLM-5.2 by Nvidia (nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4) on our own infrastructure and rerouted the entire pipeline through it, with the added benefit of keeping the attacker data on-prem. The first target was the dead-drop payloads: with GLM-5.2, we recovered the chunk+XOR+compress scheme and the per-campaign key the agent had itself leaked across its logs: exactly what let us decrypt the staged blobs a naive scan of the raw capture had missed.

GLM-5.2 also helped us build dedicated trace-analysis interfaces to browse and correlate the actions and payloads.

Sources indicate that the disclosure post covers the response at a high level. For the technical hardening:.

Recent findings suggest that the agent's offensive capability was real. This evaluation deliberately disabled OpenAI's production safety classifiers and reduced cyber refusals to measure the underlying model's raw capability. No human directed the individual steps. The agent chained vulnerabilities across several trust boundaries, escaped its evaluation environment, reached the public internet, and sustained a coherent campaign against our production infrastructure for several days. Each short-lived code evaluation environment started from scratch, yet the agent rebuilt its tooling, recovered its channels, and continued.

The individual weaknesses were familiar. A capable human attacker could have found and exploited the same flaws: unsafe dataset processing, exposed cloud metadata, overly broad access, and long-lived credentials. The agent explored them at a different scale. It took 17,600 actions, tested many paths that failed, switched channels when they were blocked, and repeatedly returned to earlier leads. Most actions went nowhere. Together, however, they produced enough coverage to find a viable chain across several independent systems.

Volume is what changes the defensive problem. We were not dealing with one clever exploit or a clean sequence of attacker actions. They had to correlate thousands of low-signal events across several systems while the agent continued testing upcoming paths. The successful path was hidden inside the noise generated by the thousands of failed ones. The same scale changed the investigation: reconstructing 17,600 actions by hand was impractical, and we had to rebuild the timeline, decode the payloads, and inventory the exposed credentials using an AI-assisted pipeline of our own.

In a recent development, our learning from this type of attack is that machine-speed offense makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive for defenders. LLM agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret. On the other hand, many parts of cybersecurity defense remain the same, and the defensive priorities remain concrete: strict isolation around evaluations, narrow trust boundaries, short-lived credentials, blocked metadata access, and detection capable of promptly correlating activity across systems to keep up.

Questions: security@huggingface.co.

One thing this timeline reinforced for me is that we still don’t have good visibility into an agent’s execution surface. We spend a lot of time discussing prompts, planning and model behaviour, but much less time asking a simple engineering question: “What consequential actions can this agent actually perform?” Once an agent can write files, invoke shell commands, modify cloud resources or make authenticated API calls, understanding and constraining that execution surface feels just as notable as evaluating the model itself.

A good gateway setup can capture most of the telemetry needed to trace an agent's actual execution and calls (and not so much the reasoning piece, which doesn't always directly correlate to the action taken): gateway the model calls, gateway the tool calls, propagate one ID through both, hash the context spans, then add kernel-level exec capture. The reasoning layer comes last and buys the least.

Industry observers note that one thing that struck me is that most of the recommendations focus on making models or existing defences better. Those are crucial, but they still leave the model holding implicit authority over real-world actions.

I wonder if we need to move the trust boundary instead. Rather than asking “did the model decide correctly?”, ask “does this action have explicit authority to execute?” If every consequential action (shell, filesystem, cloud APIs, payments, emails, etc.) had to cross an independent execution boundary that could verify authority before it happened, then improving models becomes one layer of defence rather than the only layer.

That feels like a more fundamental architectural shift than simply adding more safeguards to the model itself.

Great post! There's a lot of stuff to take in here.

One thing that's applicable to many developers is that it demonstrates some of the risks of storing secret/sensitive configuration in environment variables. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, and a malicious child process can run env or look in /proc/[PID]/environ to see them.

It's fine for dev, but shouldn't be done in prod. On a Linux system, systemd has some abstractions to properly deal with secrets (https://systemd.io/CREDENTIALS/ ). Most importantly, the secrets aren't visible to any other process (using mount namespacing), nor are they automatically passed to child processes. Access control is implemented in the kernel itself, and encryption can be handled a bunch of ways - using a key on a TPM chip, on disk, passed in via SMBIOS OEM strings, via a Cloud Instance Metadata Services (IMDS), etc.

Of course, there's other solutions for secret management too.

A leitura da timeline técnica oficial da Hugging Face traz o choque de sobriedade que faltava ao debate: não foi ficção científica, foi falha básica de isolamento e fronteira de execução.Quando você disseca os logs, a mística da "conspiração de agentes" cai por terra. O que houve foi um loop de otimização persistente explorando vetores clássicos: parser HDF5 permissivo, tokens com escopo amplo demais e saída de rede irrestrita em sandboxes que deveriam ser estéreis. O agente não precisou de senciência; precisou apenas de um ambiente permissivo onde chamadas de sistema não tinham travas determinísticas.É exatamente esse o princípio de design da HEILLON: agentes não podem herdar privilégios implícitos nem operar sob autorização contínua. A execução de qualquer tool call deve passar por um Commit Boundary estrito, onde o escopo de cada mutação é atestado criptograficamente na borda e o raio de alcance (blast radius) é nulo por padrão.Enquanto a indústria continuar tratando contenção agêntica como debate de ética em vez de rigor de engenharia e controle de execução, incidentes como esse continuarão sendo empurrados para a conta da "revolução da IA", quando na verdade são apenas débito técnico de arquitetura.

I spent some time with this timeline and with Tailscale's later write-up, and the part that stuck with me is what that stolen enrollment key actually was.

Industry observers note that it wasn't a Tailscale vulnerability. The key did what it was designed to do: enroll a node into the mesh with the reach already assigned to a CI identity. That's network membership, not access to one named service. After a rooted production node had already joined, the agent made 181 more enrollments from an external sandbox. From there it could see what that identity was allowed to reach, and it did use those routes, including traffic out through the company's exit nodes and source control through the connector its tag allowed. Hugging Face found no evidence those enrolled nodes were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API, which matters. The credential still let the agent place 181 nodes on the network.

Tailscale's own advice is the right starting point: prefer workload identity federation over a reusable automation key, and keep enrollment narrower when a key is still needed. I would also ask a prior question: did the job need network membership at all, or did it need one service?

I wrote up the longer version here: https://thirp.net/field-notes/the-credential-that-became-a-network/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maine's Gambling Control Unit is heading toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos after a single public hearing. A former lawmaker warns that the state's behavioral health system is too thin for a possible rise in gambling addiction, while a federal lawsuit still targets the tribes' exclusivity.

Industry observers note that maine’s regulator is moving toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos. Only one public hearing has been held so far. WGME’s I-Team reported on Nov. 16 that the Gambling Control Unit began iGaming rulemaking in June. Residents in the report raised a separate concern. They worry the state lacks the mental health and problem-gambling resources to cope.

Maine will become the eighth state with legal online casinos. Its four Wabanaki tribes hold exclusive licenses under LD 1164, the Wabanaki internet gaming act. The Legislature lists the measure as enacted as Public Law 538.

According to recent reports, the money set aside for addiction services is small next to the state’s cut. The legislative fiscal note sends 2% of adjusted gross iGaming receipts to the Gambling Addiction Prevention and Treatment Fund. The state’s own 18% share is projected at $1.8 million in fiscal 2025-26 and $3.6 million in fiscal 2026-27.

Critics doubt the system can absorb the demand. Patty Locuratolo Hymanson, a neurologist and former state lawmaker, told WGME that Maine lacks the behavioral health resources to handle a possible rise in gambling addiction from online casinos.

Lawmakers reshaped the revenue split before passage. A committee amendment raised the state’s share from 16% to 18%. The same amendment cut the opioid treatment fund’s allocation from 3% to 1.5%. The fiscal note also carries ongoing General Fund appropriations of $645,354 for six Gambling Control Unit positions. Those include two criminal intelligence analysts and two auditors.

It has been revealed that the regulator itself was skeptical at first. Before the bill became law, Executive Director Milt Champion opposed it in written testimony. He argued iGaming wasn’t warranted while sports wagering was only in its second year.

It has been revealed that rulemaking is still underway. The unit issued its third version of the draft rules on Sept. 30, 2026, and took comments until Oct. 30. Champion has warned that major revisions would force a fourth publication. The third draft keeps the tax rate on adjusted gross receipts unchanged. It also retains the license fee and bond requirements. The regulator is hiring six staff members dedicated to iGaming.

Sources indicate that the launch also faces a court fight over tribal exclusivity. Churchill Downs and Oxford Casino Hotel brought their suit against the Gambling Control Unit and Champion in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine. They are asking the court to declare the law unconstitutional. The challenge goes to the heart of the market’s design, which reserves online casino licenses for the tribes.

The next deadlines are procedural. Under Maine’s rulemaking law, the unit has up to 120 days after comments close to adopt the rules. The Attorney General’s office has up to 150 days from that same date to approve them as legal. The unit’s rulemaking page also lists a public hearing notice marked Nov. 30, 2026, which could change that timetable.

Recent findings suggest that email remains an important communication channel for web applications. From account verification and password resets to product announcements and customer notifications, many applications depend on email to keep users informed.

Industry observers note that for developers, however, implementing email functionality involves more than connecting a service and sending a message. A reliable email system needs to handle authentication, dynamic content, delivery failures, user preferences, event tracking, and integrations with other application components.

Using an email service provider (ESP) can simplify this process. Most modern providers offer REST APIs, SMTP relays, templates, automation features, and reporting tools that developers can integrate into existing applications.

This guide explores the technical considerations involved in building email integrations, including API-based sending, webhook handling, automation workflows, and deliverability.

There are two common ways to connect an application to an email delivery service: SMTP and REST APIs.

According to recent reports, SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a standard protocol used to transfer email messages between servers. Developers can connect an application to an SMTP server using credentials and configuration settings.

REST APIs provide another approach. Instead of communicating through an email server protocol, an application sends HTTP requests to an endpoint. The provider processes the request and returns a response.

Both methods can support transactional and application-generated emails, but their implementation differs.

An application already supports SMTP configuration.

Developers want a relatively straightforward integration.

Existing frameworks or libraries provide built-in SMTP support.

An application needs programmatic control over email operations.

Developers want structured responses and error handling.

Email functionality needs to integrate with other application services.

The system requires event tracking or additional API capabilities.

The right approach depends on the application's architecture, expected email volume, and integration requirements.

An API integration allows an application to trigger emails in response to specific events.

For example, an ecommerce application might send an order confirmation after a successful payment. A SaaS application could send an account verification message after registration.

A typical integration follows this process:.

The application detects an event.

The backend prepares the recipient and message data.

The backend authenticates with the email provider.

The provider processes the request.

The application records the response and handles any errors.

Consider a Node.js application that needs to trigger an email campaign through an API.

Some platforms, including Mailmodo, provide REST API functionality for triggering campaigns and integrating external applications with email workflows.

The following example demonstrates the general structure of an HTTP request using a campaign-triggering endpoint:.

This example uses the documented Mailmodo trigger endpoint and request structure. The campaign ID and API key must be replaced with the values from the relevant account.

Notice that the API key is loaded from an environment variable rather than written directly into the source code.

Recent findings suggest that this is an key security practice. Credentials should never be exposed in frontend JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side application bundles.

Not every email provider offers the same integration capabilities. Developers should evaluate providers based on their API documentation, authentication methods, supported endpoints, event notifications, and integration flexibility.

For example, Elastic Email provides a REST API that developers can use to send emails and manage different email operations from an application.

Industry observers note that its API uses HTTPS requests and API-key authentication. Developers can use the available endpoints to send messages, manage campaigns, retrieve information, and configure webhook notifications.

When evaluating an email API, consider these technical requirements:.

Authentication: Check how API keys are generated, stored, restricted, and rotated.

Documentation: Look for clear endpoint descriptions, request examples, response formats, and error codes.

SDK availability: Official libraries can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Permission management: Separate credentials for sending emails and accessing account information can reduce unnecessary exposure.

API limitations: Review connection limits, request timeouts, rate limits, and account-level restrictions before deploying an integration.

A provider with extensive features is not necessarily the best option for every project. The important consideration is whether its API supports the application's actual requirements.

Industry observers note that sending an email is only one part of the communication process. Applications may also need to know what happens after a message is submitted.

This is where webhooks become useful.

A webhook allows an external service to send an HTTP notification to an application when a particular event occurs.

Depending on the provider, events may include:.

For example, an application could receive a delivery-failure notification and enhancement the corresponding email record in its database.

A basic Express.js webhook endpoint might look like this:.

Industry observers note that this is a simplified example rather than a complete provider-specific webhook implementation. A production endpoint should validate the provider's signature or other authentication mechanism and follow its documented payload structure.

Industry observers note that it should also handle duplicate events safely. Webhook providers may retry notifications when an application does not respond successfully.

An idempotent event handler prevents the same notification from creating duplicate database updates or triggering repeated actions.

Email automation connects application events with predefined communication sequences.

Instead of manually sending every message, developers can create workflows that respond to user activity.

Consider a SaaS application with the following registration process:.

The backend stores the latest user.

A verification email is triggered.

If the user does not complete onboarding, a follow-up message may be triggered.

A simplified workflow can be represented as:.

In a production application, email delivery should generally be handled through a background job queue rather than blocking the registration request.

A queue also makes it easier to retry temporary failures, manage sending volume, and prevent email delays from affecting the main application.

Developers should consider tools such as Redis-backed queues or framework-specific job processors when building larger systems.

Automation platforms can also help manage more complex journeys. For instance, a developer can connect application events to an external email workflow instead of implementing every communication sequence independently.

The key is to keep business logic in the application while using the email service to manage message delivery and relevant campaign operations.

A successful API response does not necessarily mean that an email has reached the recipient's inbox.

Email deliverability depends on several technical factors, including domain authentication, sender reputation, message quality, and recipient engagement.

Developers should pay attention to the following configurations.

Sender Policy Framework identifies the mail servers authorized to send messages on behalf of a domain.

A correctly configured SPF record helps receiving servers evaluate whether an email originates from an authorized source.

Sources indicate that domainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages. Receiving servers can use the corresponding public key in DNS to verify the signature.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance builds on SPF and DKIM. It allows domain owners to publish policies for handling messages that fail authentication checks and receive reports about authentication activity.

These three mechanisms should be configured carefully, especially when an application sends emails through multiple providers.

Sources indicate that email systems generate useful operational data. However, developers should avoid treating every available metric as an accurate measure of user engagement.

According to recent reports, for example, open tracking can be affected by privacy features and automated image loading. Click tracking may also include automated security scans.

More reliable application-level signals can include:.

These events can be connected with email campaign data to understand how communication affects application activity.

Developers should also maintain a clear separation between email delivery records and user account records. This makes it easier to investigate delivery concerns without unnecessarily modifying customer data.

When collecting engagement information, applications should follow applicable privacy requirements and respect user communication preferences.

Before deploying an email integration, developers should review the following areas:.

API security: Store credentials in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.

Domain authentication: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

Error handling: Account for failed requests, invalid recipients, and temporary provider errors.

Background processing: Use queues for asynchronous email delivery.

Webhook validation: Verify incoming notifications and handle duplicate events.

Monitoring: Track delivery failures, bounce rates, and application-level outcomes.

Testing: Test email templates across different clients and devices before production deployment.

These practices help create an email system that is easier to maintain, troubleshoot, and scale.

Email integration is an crucial part of modern application development, but a reliable implementation requires more than connecting an SMTP server or calling an API endpoint.

Developers need to consider authentication, asynchronous processing, webhook security, automation logic, domain configuration, and event monitoring.

REST APIs are useful for applications that need programmatic control over email operations, while SMTP remains a practical option for systems that already support standard mail-server connections. Webhooks add another layer by allowing applications to respond to delivery events and upgrade their internal records.

By choosing an integration method that fits the application architecture and following sound security and deliverability practices, developers can build email functionality that supports both immediate communication needs and long-term application growth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence.
  • In practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths.
  • Recent findings suggest that our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence. In LLM RL, the model serves as the policy, π(action | previous tokens), and true on-policy learning requires every action in an update to be generated and evaluated by that exact same policy. While a synchronous loop ensures each rollout batch is scored using the same weights that generated it, a critical numerical requirement remains: the sampler and trainer must evaluate that policy identically.

In practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths. The sampler chooses each action token during incremental decoding and records its behavior logprob. The trainer evaluates the same token in batched forward-backward passes to compute its current logprob and gradients. Under the same weights, these differing execution paths can still assign different logprobs to the same token and context. The training schedule is on-policy, but the numerical execution has introduced a hidden off-policy gap that compounds over multi-turn trajectories.

Recent findings suggest that our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

  • Realistically, even long-time Nest consumers have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

It has been revealed that the Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest consumers have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

In a recent development, having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a big fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That remarked, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

Google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

The Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped.
  • In a recent development, pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record.
  • iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

In a recent development, pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

According to recent reports, two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

Industry observers note that october was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

Recent findings suggest that the October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

Sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split showed up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

The record arrives as Harrisburg weighs a gaming modernization package. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced House Bill 2801 with four co-sponsors. On September 24, 2026, it was referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee. Titled ‘Skill Games & Gaming Modernization,’ the bill would rewrite large parts of the state’s gaming code.

Your accessibility check in CI is green. axe-core ran, zero violations, and the badge in the README looks great. Your site can still fail WCAG 2.2.

Sources indicate that that isn't a bug in axe. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. It added nine success criteria and dropped one (4.1.1 Parsing), and most of the fresh ones can't be judged by reading the DOM. Deque remarked as much when it shipped the first WCAG 2.2 support in axe-core 4.5: the target-size rule would probably be the only new-criterion rule they added, because the others can't be automated without a lot of false positives.

So the rest is on you. This article covers the one criterion axe can check and three it can't (focus not obscured, dragging movements, accessible authentication), with Playwright tests you can drop into a project. I ran all of them against a small test page that fails every criterion on purpose, and against a fixed version of the same page. If you want a plain-language rundown of every change first, WCAG 2.2 vs 2.1 goes through them. Here I only care about what you can put in a pipeline.

Level A and AA are what most contracts and laws point at, so those are the ones that matter first. The AAA criteria are still worth knowing about.

In a recent development, that's four AA criteria with something you can script, one of which axe already handles. The rest of this article goes through those four.

The AA rule is smaller than most people expect: a pointer target should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or sit far enough from its neighbours that a 24px circle centred on it wouldn't overlap another target or that target's own circle. There are exceptions, including inline links in a sentence, and targets whose size the browser controls.

Sources indicate that axe-core has a target-size rule for this. One catch: it isn't part of a default run. In my setup (axe-core 4.14.1 through @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0), a plain analyze() on the broken page reported nothing at all. The rule only demonstrated up once I asked for it:.

According to recent reports, on the broken page this lists the three 16px toolbar buttons by selector. On the fixed page, with 32px buttons, it passes. If you've been running axe for years and never seen a target-size result, this is why.

Recent findings suggest that some context on how common the problem is. In the scan data behind my last SitePoint article, 34.5% of the 1,025 sites had controls below a stricter 44px threshold. That is a tougher standard than the 24px that AA asks for, so don't read it as "a third of sites fail 2.5.8". Plenty of those would pass. But it does show how many production sites ship tiny controls.

If you'd like a quick look at one page before wiring anything up, browser tools such as axe DevTools, WAVE, or a WCAG checker will show the same thing.

axe can't test it, because you have to press Tab and look at where the browser scrolled. Two details caught me out building this:.

According to recent reports, the check below samples a grid of points inside the visible part of the focused element and asks the browser what's on top at each one. If none of the points land on the element or its children, it's covered.

On my broken page it reported nine hits: links hidden behind the footer going forward ("Section 4 link", "Section 10 link", "Section 16 link") and the toolbar buttons and a few links hidden behind the header coming back. The output names the element and the key, which is what you want when you're staring at a failed build.

The fix is one CSS rule, sized to your sticky elements:.

That tells the browser to leave room when it scrolls a focused element into view. With it in place the same test passes.

Recent findings suggest that be aware of what this can't see: a modal that opens over the page, or a chat widget that only appears after a delay, will not show up unless your test opens or waits for them. Adrian Roselli's piece on 2.4.11 and adversarial conformance is worth reading for the awkward cases.

Anything you can do by dragging needs a way to do it with a single click or tap, unless dragging is essential. Sortable lists, sliders, kanban cards, file reorderers: all of them.

Sources indicate that you can't prove a drag alternative works from a script. But you can catch the obvious mistake, which is a draggable item with no button anywhere near it:.

The limit is real. It only recognises the native draggable attribute. Libraries built on pointer events, such as dnd-kit, don't set it, so this test will walk right past them. If you use one of those, replace the selector with whatever your component renders, or add a test per drag component. Treat it as a tripwire for the common case, not a verdict.

The fix, in the fixed page, is a pair of "Move up" and "Move down" buttons on each item, each with an accessible name that says which item it moves.

Sources indicate that this dispatches a synthetic paste event and checks whether anything called preventDefault() on it. It catches the old onpaste="return false" trick, and it catches script-based blockers too. It does not tell you whether your login has a CAPTCHA that needs an alternative, or an emailed one-time code you must retype. Those need a person.

On a pull request, a plain GitHub Actions job is enough:.

It has been revealed that point PAGE_URL at a running preview, and run the tests against the pages that matter most: sign-in, checkout, anything with a sticky element. Don't try to crawl everything on the first pass. A test that fails for reasons nobody owns gets deleted within a month.

Four things I haven't tried to automate, and wouldn't:.

In a recent development, automation will keep the regressions out. It won't tell you the work is finished. A green build and a conformant site are different things, and WCAG 2.2 widened the gap between them.

Industry observers note that the tests and both test pages are small enough to read in one sitting. Copy what's useful, change the selectors, and keep the broken page around: it's a handy way to check that a test fails when it should.

NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

📅 27 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Surgical robotics is moving promptly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies.
  • World foundation models offer a different path.
  • Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Surgical robotics is moving promptly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Sources indicate that cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are notable: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

Recent findings suggest that the teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

It has been revealed that cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

Sources indicate that the resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Sources indicate that cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

Sources indicate that while Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a newly introduced frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a latest family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:.

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a newly introduced environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the newly introduced closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really highlights how challenging this field is. 👏.

Recent findings suggest that it’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱.

In a recent development, looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI has birthed some truly colossal supers, they just aren't on the Top500.
  • For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.
  • According to recent reports, with the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI has birthed some truly colossal supers, they just aren't on the Top500.

For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.

According to recent reports, with the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name. China’s Lineshine supercomputer at 2.2 exaFLOPS of double precision compute in the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark may be the top system on the bi-annual ranking, but it’s nowhere near the biggest compute cluster in the world.

Superclusters like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, Meta’s Promethius, and OpenAI’s Stargate pack hundreds of thousands of GPUs, dwarfing anything on the Top500 today.

“These [companies] are not interested in submitting to the Top500,” Eth Zürich’s Torsten Hoefler said during his Supercomputing address this week.

According to recent reports, it’s a dilemma that the founders of the Top500 ranking are now grappling with. And some believe it may be time for a rethink.

“What’s really needed for tracking that more appropriately is not just a different benchmark but also different methodology,” Top500 author Erich Strohmaier said.

For a long time, Strohmaier explains, compute capability was roughly aligned with capacity.

According to recent reports, what happened in the last few years with AI is “capacity really pulled ahead of capability in terms of market size,” he stated. “We were and we still are very focused on capability.”.

By capability, Strohmaier is referring to the ability to run one code across the entire cluster.

“Our prime rule for benchmarking is, you have to benchmark your whole system with one code and you cannot just add two parts up to make up a number,” he explained.

Industry observers note that this is problematic for the large clusters major hyperscalers and cloud providers are now building to fuel the AI boom. “All those systems are capacity systems,” Strohmaier remarked.

In the age of AI, the top spot on the bi-annual ranking is whoever willing to run HPL instead of LLMs.

They’re not designed to run one piece of code but have instead been architected to run many, many smaller or medium-sized code instantiations, which may include training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and of course inference.

Because of this, Strohmaier states, it wouldn’t be reasonable to expect SpaceXAI to run something High-Performance Linpack (HPL) on a cluster like Colossus.

But these clusters are still worth tracking. They'll just need a new benchmark better suited to judging the capability of these arrays while at the same time preventing operators from gaming the system.

What shape or form such a benchmark might take remains to be seen. Developing a new benchmark or methodology is no small task, and changing the existing benchmarks isn’t ideal. ”If we do anything to the benchmark itself, we’re going to lose the historic trends, which is extremely valuable,” Hoefler said.

Allowing for lower precisions — HPL-MxP already does this to some extent — is one avenue for addressing the fact that these accelerators are increasingly trading FP64 performance for lower-accuracy floating-point data types like FP8 or FP4.

Industry observers note that another avenue is developing a separate AI benchmark. This would be immediately applicable to these clusters, but with the pace of change in model architecture, building such a benchmark is challenging.

According to recent reports, “The AI workloads change every two weeks, so if you pick something today, it’s going to be irrelevant in at most a year, and these benchmarks need to live for multiple decades,” Hoefler said. ®.

#69739. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the Upcoming Grounded Aircraft
